tone_statements.citation: Fernández de Miranda, María Teresa. 1965. Los préstamos españoles en el zapoteco de Mitla. Anales del Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia 17 (1964): 259-273. México: INAH. Open PDF:https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/663e/a6a8287f6734a97facc69b55e572980d02db.pdf
tone_statements.quote: El zapoteco de Mitla posee veintiseis consonantes divididas en tres grupos: ... y seis vocales i, e, æ, a, o, u. Es un idioma tonal con dos tonos de nivel y dos deslizamientos que se presentan sobre vocales sencillas: alto (´), bajo (sin representar), alto-bajo (ˆ) y bajo-alto (ˇ). El acento no es fonémico, siempre se encuentra en las sílabas finales de radical.
tone_statements.translation: Mitla Zapotec has twenty-six consonants divided into three groups: ... and six vowels i, e, æ, a, o, u. It is a tonal language with two level tones and two glides that occur on single vowels: high (´), low (unmarked), high-low (ˆ) and low-high (ˇ). Stress is not phonemic; it always falls on the final syllables of the radical.
tone_statements.summary: Four tonemes (high, low, high-low glide, low-high glide) on vowels; non-phonemic radical-final stress; sketch from Briggs 1961 Mitla Zapotec Grammar. Sec. 2.3 summarises Briggs's tone sandhi (mostly low>high, progressive and regressive) and gives tone rules for the 365 Spanish loans in the index.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: no Briggs 1961 file is. the deciding Briggs pp.7-8 wording is search-snippet evidence and could not be re-verified today (Google Books captcha, archive.org offline). (2) But the held Stubblefield & Hollenbach 1991 SIL grammar sketch, read from page scan, states the same system at page grade: word accent falls on the final ROOT; complex vowels survive only under stress; 3sg -ni, 1pl -nu and the enclitic adverbs are unstressed; root-like 'dependent adverbs' (-ro, -gajc, -duxh..) take the stress as last root of a compound. This matches the record's domain statement (stem-final, word-final only when the word ends in its stem; compounds stressed on the last stem) and the morph-split/dominant-final handling. One refinement not in the record: 1sg -ä takes the word stress after a broken or aspirated root vowel (baslaä 'solté') but not after a checked vowel (§0.3) — a suffix-specif

sources.quote: p. 7: "Stress in Mitla Zapoteco is non-phonemic; stress occurs on stem-final syllables in all words studied. The placement of stress in Mitla Zapoteco seems contrary to that of other Zapoteco languages, which may have stress occurring on other syllables than the stem-final one." Corroborating p. 3: "... a lowered allotone in final un-stressed syllable: ge?-ni 'it is lime', bya?N-lu 'you stayed', ba.wi 'look', gu.läb-ni 'it boiled'."

sources.quote: §0.2: 'El acento prosódico de la palabra cae sobre la raíz final, y las vocales complejas (las no sencillas) se presentan solamente en las sílabas acentuadas. Así que, las vocales complejas se cambian por las vocales sencillas correspondientes cuando se presentan en las sílabas no finales de las palabras compuestas ... -ro grande y -gajc luego son raíces, y producen un cambio de la vocal, mientras que el pronombre inseparable -ni tercera persona no provoca ningún cambio.'
